Pages: one site through gh-pages-multiplexer, with PR previews

Main and landscape publish together as one version per ref: main/ on main, pr-<n>/ per pull request,
with the landscape under landscape/ inside each. The sticky preview comment links the PR's version.

Landscape: committed page data, Pages ships the explorer

The survey's export output is committed, so CI builds the page from the repo alone. The page
derives the GitHub link and the kind label instead of storing them: the page is 2.3 MB from 2.7.
The Pages workflow builds the explorer and publishes it under /landscape/ beside the main site.

Landscape page: bars and project detail load per bundle, one build script

The page is 2.7 MB (from 10.8 MB). Bar frames and each project's long text are written as
script bundles beside the page and loaded when a project is opened. explorer/build.sh runs the
export, type check and bundle in order.

Survey: 2,091 bars from the safe and review tiers; top 300 from 61 to 125

The review tier runs under the same sandbox, since every signal that put a project
there is one the sandbox and fake home contain. Dependencies fetched for 331
failing safe projects and the entry guessing reworked recovered 201 more. The
process README records what the sweeps taught.

Survey capture: each project runs in its own child runner with a hard limit

A bar's helper put the runner into an uninterruptible wait that no pipe handling
inside the process could escape, and three escaped daemons from one project
outlived their sweep by an hour. With no slugs given, the runner now drives a
child per project in its own session, kills it at fifteen minutes, and records the
project as having stalled.

Survey capture: venv on the sandbox's python, manifest entries as fallback, no wait on escaped daemons

deps.py builds venvs on the Homebrew python3, since uv's managed interpreter lives
under the home directory the sandbox denies. resolve.py uses a package.json bin or
main as a fallback entry, mapping an unbuilt dist path to its src, and weights a
statusline-named file above cli or index. run.py stops a timeline whose ticks
average over three seconds, and after a timeout closes the pipes instead of
waiting on them, which hung a worker for an hour when a bar's daemon had made its
own session.

Survey: capture process doc, dependency fetch, better entry guessing, review tier runs

resolve.py ranks the survey's files by reading stdin and entry-like names, runs a
module inside a Python package as a module, reads a shebang for an extensionless
file, keeps the author's runner when they named one, and takes the tiers to run as
arguments. deps.py fetches npm and Python dependencies on the host without running
any package code. run.py ends each tick's process group. The README in
tools/capture is the process: order, traps, decisions, and where the sweeps stand.

Survey: bars play through a two-minute mock conversation, with speed, deep-link history and live markers

The capture runner walks every safe project through a fixture timeline of sixty
ticks (hook JSON, transcript, working tree) at 80, 120 and 160 columns and keeps
each frame the output changed to. The page inflates the frames from a gzip blob
and plays them off one shared clock with a speed control. Projects with a bar
are marked teal in the graph, the search and the lists. Each opened node is a
history entry so back walks through them. Links pull in proportion to degree so
a crowded characteristic is held rather than hauled into a knot.

The sandbox now also denies /tmp and the user temp directory, the fixture ships
a real git so Apple's xcrun shim does not stall, and scrub.py rewrites the host's
user, host and run path out of every captured frame.

Survey: capture 1,143 statuslines in a sandbox and replay them in the explorer

A risk triage stamps every project from a read of its statusline files; the
safe tier runs under sandbox-exec against one fake session at three widths,
and the explorer draws the selected project's bar along the bottom in xterm.js.

Survey: the 1,000 most-committed Claude Code statuslines — clones, new ideas, why so many

Ranks the styling survey's 9,558 projects by commits, reads the top 1,000
from source with haiku agents, fingerprints their code for copies, and
answers whether they are clones, what is new in them, and why there are
so many. README.md has the answers; projects.md and projects.tsv hold one
entry per project; tools/ holds the scripts and agent briefs.
